messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The explosion came without warning. Kiet was forty-two then, a firefighter who had volunteered for a six-week relief deployment after a humanitarian crisis in a neighboring region. He had been trained to run toward danger, to pull people from rubble, to triage the wounded in the chaos of collapsed buildings. What he had not been trained for was the quiet that followed. After the shelling stopped, he helped dig bodies from a schoolyard. He held a child whose legs were gone. He watched a man—another relief worker—turn away from a dying woman because she was from the wrong village. That moment, the moral violation of it, lodged in Kiet’s chest like a piece of shrapnel he could not feel but knew was there. He came home, returned to his station, tried to resume his life. His marriage, already strained, dissolved within two years. He told no one what he had seen.

Now, at forty-six, Kiet lives alone in a small apartment near the firehouse. He works the overnight shift when he can, because the silence of the day is unbearable. When the station is quiet between calls, he feels a pressure building in his ears, a certainty that something dangerous is about to happen. He has come to believe that silence itself is a threat, a prelude to catastrophe. This belief began during the deployment, when the quiet before an attack was always the worst part, but it has since attached itself to every still moment in his life. At the grocery store, in the hallway of his building, during the lull between radio transmissions—he scans for exits, for signs of trouble, for the sound of a bang that will confirm his dread.

The bang itself is the worst trigger. A car backfiring, a door slamming, a dropped pan in the station kitchen—each one sends a jolt of physical pain through his ribs and his left arm, exactly where he felt the shockwave during the explosion that leveled the schoolyard. The memory returns with the pain, but it is never in order. He sees the dust, then the child’s face, then the overturned desk, then the man who walked away—but he cannot sequence them. He knows what happened, but when he tries to describe it to the department psychologist, the words dissolve. He cannot find a sentence that holds the truth of it. This inability to speak, to sequence, to make the memory obey him, has convinced Kiet that he acted in ways that go against who he is. He believes his life has been destroyed by that deployment. He feels he no longer belongs anywhere—not at the station, not with his ex-wife, not among civilians who have never seen what he saw. He is certain that the moral failure he witnessed, and his own helplessness in that moment, have made him unfit for any world he once inhabited.

These appraisals drive him to desperate strategies. When the guilt and shame become unbearable, Kiet hurts himself physically to release the overwhelming feelings. He will press his knuckles into the edge of a table until the skin breaks, or dig his nails into his palms during a long silence at the station. He has also developed mental rituals he must perform to prevent bad things from happening again—counting the beats of his heart in sets of four, repeating a phrase under his breath before opening a door, touching the same three surfaces in his locker before he can leave. He tries hard not to think about the trauma, but the suppression only makes the memories more insistent. The rituals and the suppression, in turn, make the threat feel more real; when he cannot complete a ritual, his anxiety spikes, and he becomes irritable, snapping at younger firefighters for minor mistakes. He has been written up twice for angry outbursts.

The cycle tightens. A comment about sexual violence on the evening news triggers the memory of the man who turned away from the dying woman, and Kiet’s stomach clenches with the physical pain of that moment. He then believes, again, that he is complicit in that violation by having done nothing. The belief drives him to hurt himself that night, and the self-harm, briefly numbing, is followed by a wave of new shame and a renewed sense that he is dangerous to be around. He has stopped accepting invitations to crew dinners. He no longer calls his brother. The silence in his apartment grows deeper, and he is certain something terrible is about to happen again.

What finally brought Kiet to seek help was a single moment at the station. A new recruit dropped a steel pan in the kitchen, and Kiet, without thinking, threw a chair across the room. The recruit was unharmed, but the look on his face—fear, not of the bang, but of Kiet—broke something open in him. He called the department psychologist the next morning. He is terrified that he will hurt someone else, that he will be asked to leave the only job he has ever loved, and that the silence that follows will finally prove him right: that he belongs nowhere, not even here.
